svg.title: Mobile remote — pairing a phone, and the channel through the relay
svg.desc: Sequence diagram with seven lifelines: you at the desktop, the dialog Settings › Remote access, the remote bridge in the desktop's main process, the relay's Cloud Functions, the relay's Realtime Database, the iPhone app, and you with the phone. Phase 1, open a pairing: the desktop creates identity keys once and a pairing secret that never leaves the machine, registers a channel and a five-minute one-use pairing at the relay, and only then shows the QR code with the typed key; without a claim in five minutes, or on Cancel, the pairing and the channel are deleted. Phase 2, scan and claim: the phone scans the code, creates its keys in the Secure Enclave, fetches the desktop's public keys, sends its own public keys with an HMAC over both under the pairing secret, and the relay links them to the channel, refusing any second key. Phase 3, confirm in person: the desktop checks the HMAC, both sides show the same six-word safety phrase, and only a click on Allow in the native sheet of the confirmation port completes the pairing; the desktop sends its own MAC, the relay sets the channel to paired and the phone checks that MAC. The words come from one fixed list in every language. Phase 4, connect: on every start both sides get a token by a signed challenge, mark their presence, run an X25519 handshake through the database and derive session keys; from then on every message is an encrypted envelope in the other side's outbox, which the relay can carry but not read. Phase 5, end: Remove phone deletes the channel, and the phone deletes its keys. Three points were added to the concept on 2026-10-18: the outboxes stay closed until the channel is paired, the desktop sends a confirmation MAC that the phone checks, and the desktop's presence is a heartbeat because REST streaming has no onDisconnect.

Numbers are steps, top to bottom. R1, R8: ground rules of the mobile remote concept. #980: confirmation port with user presence. Keys: P-256 identity keys per side (sign, agree); desktopKeys and phoneKeys are their public halves.
